---
title: "Quiz: projections and the sinogram"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Lines are $x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho$, origin at the image centre, $y$ up, $\theta \in [0°, 180°)$.

---

**Q1.** Why does a CT scanner work with $-\ln(I/I_0)$ rather than with the measured intensity $I$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How do the attenuations of two layers combine?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each layer removes a fraction of the photons, so the transmitted fractions **multiply**. The logarithm turns the product into a **sum** of $\mu$ along the ray: a line integral, linear in the unknown attenuation. All reconstruction methods rely on that linearity.
:::

---

**Q2.** 10 cm of water-like tissue ($\mu = 0.2$ cm⁻¹): what fraction of the photons gets through? And with 1 cm of bone ($\mu = 0.5$ cm⁻¹) added?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$I/I_0 = e^{-\sum \mu\,\Delta s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$e^{-2} = 0.135$, about 14 %. With the bone: $e^{-2.5} = 0.082$; the bone alone would pass $e^{-0.5} = 0.61$, and the two fractions multiply: $0.135 \cdot 0.61 = 0.082$.
:::

---

**Q3.** What does the projection at $\theta = 0°$ of an image look like, in terms of its pixels? And at $\theta = 90°$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At $\theta = 0°$ the lines are $x = \rho$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At $0°$ the rays are vertical: the projection is the **column sums**, left to right with increasing $\rho$. At $90°$ the rays are horizontal: the **row sums**, with the top row at the largest $\rho$ (because $y$ points up).
:::

---

**Q4.** A sinogram contains a sinusoid with amplitude 30 pixels whose maximum is at $\theta = 60°$. Where is the point?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\rho = r\cos(\theta - \varphi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At distance $r = 30$ from the centre in direction $\varphi = 60°$: $(30\cos 60°, 30\sin 60°) = (15, 26)$.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is a half turn (180°) enough for a parallel-beam scanner?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the rays at $\theta$ and at $\theta + 180°$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The line at $(\theta + 180°, \rho)$ is the line at $(\theta, -\rho)$: the same set of points. So $p_{\theta + 180°}(\rho) = p_\theta(-\rho)$; the second half turn repeats the first, mirrored.
:::

---

**Q6.** The sums of the projections of a scan are 512.3 at most angles but 480.1 at a few neighbouring angles. What might have happened?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which number should every projection share?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every projection should sum to the total of the object. A drop at a few angles means those projections lost part of the object: for example, the object stuck out of the field of view at those angles (truncation), or detector elements failed, or the source fluctuated. The consistency check catches it.
:::

---

**Q7.** You move an object 10 pixels up (in $+y$). How does its sinogram change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each point moves by $\mathbf t\cdot(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ on the detector.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every point's curve moves by $10\sin\theta$: not at all at $0°$ (vertical rays do not see a vertical shift), by $+10$ at $90°$, and back to $0$ at $180°$. The whole sinogram is bent by this sinusoid; it is not simply shifted.
:::

---

**Q8.** Row sums and column sums of a binary image are known. Why can't you always reconstruct the image from them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look for a change that keeps every row and column sum.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Swapping a $2 \times 2$ checkerboard pattern $\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix} \leftrightarrow \begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}$ (in any two rows and two columns) leaves all row and column sums unchanged. Different images give the same two projections; more angles are needed to tell them apart.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that every projection of $f$ has the same integral $\int p_\theta(\rho)\,d\rho$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\int p_\theta(\rho)\,d\rho = \iint f(\rho\,\mathbf n_\theta + s\,\mathbf n_\theta^\perp)\,ds\,d\rho$. The map $(\rho, s) \mapsto \rho\,\mathbf n_\theta + s\,\mathbf n_\theta^\perp$ is a rotation with Jacobian 1, so the double integral is $\iint f\,dx\,dy$, independent of $\theta$.
:::
